\chapter{El Cuerpo Y El Descanso}
\label{ch:es-cuerpo}
\hlchaptermodality{438}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say where I exercise, report an injury the way a clinic expects to hear it, say I have to rest, and close the story by laughing about it.}

Read the notice or message this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el polideportivo]{el polideportivo — one roof, many sports}

\label{lesson:ES-C438-polideportivo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el deporte} and \textbf{el gimnasio}. A gimnasio holds one room of machines. Now picture a building that holds a pool, a court and a running track at once.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el polideportivo}
\textbf{el polideportivo} — the municipal sports centre.

Every town of any size has one, and its sign is the one you read to find out what the pool costs and when the court is free. It is a \textbf{deporte} word, so it is masculine: \emph{el polideportivo}, \emph{los polideportivos}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Three pieces, and the middle one is already yours.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{where it comes from} \\
\midrule
\textbf{poli-} & Greek \emph{polýs}, many \\
\textbf{deportiv-} & from \textbf{deporte}, sport \\
\textbf{-o} & masculine ending \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Many-sport-place.} Spanish did not borrow this word from anywhere; it built it, in the twentieth century, out of a Greek prefix and a Latin stem, because town councils needed a name for a thing that did not exist before.

That Greek \textbf{poli-} is the same one inside \emph{polígono} and \emph{poliglota}. It is not the \emph{poli-} of \emph{policía}, which is a different Greek word entirely — \emph{pólis}, the city. Two prefixes that look identical and mean nothing like each other.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el polideportivo}
  \item the difference between a gimnasio and a polideportivo
  \item what the piece \emph{poli-} is doing in the word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The sports centre? (\textbf{El polideportivo}.) What does \textbf{poli-} mean? (\textbf{Many}.) Which syllable carries the stress? (\emph{-ti-}, the second from last.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la natación]{la natación — the same root, arriving twice}

\label{lesson:ES-C438-natacion}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{nadar}. Now say \textbf{el polideportivo}. The timetable on its door does not list \emph{nadar}; it lists a noun.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la natación}
\textbf{la natación} — swimming, the activity as a named thing.

\emph{Hago natación los martes} — I swim on Tuesdays. \emph{Un curso de natación} — a swimming course. \textbf{nadar} is what your arms do; \textbf{la natación} is what the timetable, the club and the medal call it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{nat-} from Latin \emph{natāre}, to swim, plus \textbf{-ción}, the ending you met on \emph{documentación} for turning an action into a thing.

\emph{documentar} gave \emph{documentación}; \emph{natar} gives \emph{natación}. Same machine.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Here is the part worth slowing down for. \textbf{nadar} and \textbf{la natación} come from the \emph{same} Latin word, and they do not look alike. That is because they took different roads out of Latin.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the word} & \textbf{the road it took} \\
\midrule
nadar & carried in every mouth, worn smooth \\
natación & lifted off the page, centuries later \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{natāre} was spoken without a break for a thousand years, and a thousand years of speaking wore the \textbf{t} soft into a \textbf{d} and dropped a syllable: \emph{natāre} became \emph{nadar}. Then scholars who could read Latin needed a formal noun, went back to the written form, and took \emph{natātiōnem} out intact.

A pair like this is called a \textbf{doublet}: one word, two arrivals, both alive. Once you can see them, Spanish is full of them, and the learned twin is nearly always the one on the official sign.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la natación}
  \item I do swimming at the sports centre
  \item why \emph{nadar} and \emph{natación} look so different
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Swimming, the discipline? (\textbf{La natación}.) Which ending makes it a noun? (\textbf{-ción}.) Which of the twins was worn down by mouths? (\emph{Nadar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[torcerse]{torcerse — the ankle that turns the wrong way}

\label{lesson:ES-C438-torcerse}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la natación}, \textbf{el pie} and \textbf{el tobillo}. Getting out of the pool, the tiled edge is wet. Name the part of you that is about to go wrong.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: torcerse}
\textbf{torcer} — to twist something. \textbf{torcerse} — to twist a part of yourself.

\emph{Me he torcido el pie} — I have twisted my foot. This is the sentence a Spanish doctor's waiting room hears twenty times a week, and it is the one you want ready before you need it.

Spanish does not say \emph{my} foot here. It says \textbf{el} pie and lets \textbf{me} carry the ownership: \emph{me torcí \textbf{el} tobillo}, not \emph{mi tobillo}. When the body part is yours and the verb is reflexive, the possessive is redundant and Spanish drops it.

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{torquēre}, to twist. It is one of those roots that stayed busy.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the twist in it} \\
\midrule
torcer & a joint, the wrong way \\
torcido & crooked, not straight \\
antorcha & a torch, of twisted rags \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English took the same root twice over: \textbf{torque}, the twisting force on a shaft, and \textbf{torture}, which needs no explanation once you know the root.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the stem that breaks}]
\textbf{dormir} taught you that some verbs split their vowel when the stress lands on it: \emph{dormir} but \emph{duermo}. \textbf{torcer} does the same thing.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{form} & \textbf{vowel} \\
\midrule
torcer, torcemos & \textbf{o}, unstressed \\
me tuerzo, se tuerce & \textbf{ue}, stressed \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

What decides it is stress, not person. Wherever the stress falls on the stem vowel, the \textbf{o} breaks into \textbf{ue}; wherever the ending pulls the stress away, the \textbf{o} holds. That is why \emph{torcemos} keeps its \textbf{o} while \emph{tuerce} does not — and why you never have to memorise which forms change.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{torcerse}
  \item I twisted my foot at the swimming class
  \item \emph{torcemos} and \emph{se tuerce}, and why the vowel differs
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To twist your own ankle? (\textbf{Torcerse}.) What is the Latin root? (\emph{Torquēre}, to twist.) What happens to the \textbf{o} when the stress lands on it? (\textbf{It breaks into ue}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[descansar]{descansar — to un-tire yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C438-descansar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{cansado}, the word for a body with nothing left in it. Say \textbf{torcerse}. You have twisted your ankle and you are tired. Name what the doctor is about to tell you to do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: descansar}
\textbf{descansar} — to rest.

\emph{Tiene que descansar dos días} — you have to rest for two days. \emph{Descanse} on a sign at a viewpoint or a clinic is an invitation to sit. The related noun \textbf{el descanso} is what a timetable calls a break, and what a football match calls half-time.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{des-} plus \textbf{cansar}, and you already own the second half.

\emph{Cansado} came from Latin \textbf{campsāre}, which was a sailor's word: to turn a ship round a headland. Turning the ship round, over and over, was the hard work that wore a crew out, and the word slid from the manoeuvre to the exhaustion it caused.

\textbf{des-} is the undoing prefix. Put it on \textbf{cansar} and you get the reversal:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what it does to the tiredness} \\
\midrule
cansar & puts it there \\
descansar & takes it away \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
English \textbf{rest} names a condition you are in. Spanish \textbf{descansar} names an action you perform on a condition: you go in and remove the tiredness.

That is not a curiosity, it changes how the word behaves. Because it is a reversal and not a state, it takes a duration the way any action does — \emph{descansé media hora}, I rested for half an hour — where English has to reach for \emph{had a rest} to make \emph{rest} countable.

The prefix is productive, so the move is reusable. \textbf{des-} on a verb you already know gives you its undoing, and you can often guess the result before anyone teaches it to you.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{descansar}
  \item I twisted my ankle, so I have to rest
  \item what \textbf{des-} is doing to \emph{cansar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To rest? (\textbf{Descansar}.) What does \textbf{des-} do? (\textbf{Undoes}.) What was \emph{campsāre} originally about? (\textbf{Turning a ship round a headland}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[reír]{reír — the prefix that is not there}

\label{lesson:ES-C438-reir}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la risa}, the noun for the sound itself. Say \textbf{descansar}. You are resting a twisted ankle and the whole thing is faintly ridiculous. Name the verb \emph{risa} belongs to.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: reír}
\textbf{reír} — to laugh. \textbf{reírse de} — to laugh \emph{at} something.

\emph{Nos reímos mucho} — we laughed a lot. \emph{No te rías} — do not laugh. And \textbf{sonreír}, with \emph{son-} from Latin \emph{sub-}, under: a laugh kept low, which is exactly what a smile is.

\begin{cousinweb}
Here is the trap, and it is worth setting off deliberately.

\textbf{reír} looks like \textbf{re-} plus \textbf{ír}. It is neither. There is no prefix and there is no \emph{ir}. The whole word is Latin \textbf{rīdēre}, to laugh, arriving in one piece — the \emph{r-e} at the front is nothing more than the first two letters of the root.

You met \textbf{batería}, a word that wears an \emph{ending} it never earned. This is the other half of that lesson: a word that wears a \emph{prefix} it never had. Spanish has both kinds, and neither announces itself.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The written accent on \textbf{reír} is physical evidence, and you can read it.

\emph{Rīdēre} had a \textbf{d} between its vowels: \emph{ri-d-ere}. Spanish wore intervocalic \textbf{d} away in word after word, and when it went here it left the \textbf{i} and the \textbf{e} standing next to each other with nothing between them.

Two vowels side by side would normally collapse into one syllable. These do not, because they were never together — a consonant used to hold them apart. The accent on the \textbf{í} is how Spanish writes down that refusal: \emph{re-ír}, two syllables, the join still visible where the \textbf{d} used to be.

The family keeps the evidence too: \textbf{la risa} lost the same \textbf{d}, while \textbf{ridículo} was borrowed back from Latin late enough to keep it. One root, one missing consonant, and a word on each side of the loss.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{reír}
  \item we rested and we laughed a lot
  \item what the accent on the \textbf{í} is recording
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To laugh? (\textbf{Reír}.) Is the \textbf{re-} a prefix? (\textbf{No — it is part of the root}.) Which consonant fell out and left the accent behind? (\textbf{The d}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(polideportivo, natación, torcerse …]{(polideportivo, natación, torcerse, descansar, reír) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R438-repaso-cuerpo}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all five: \emph{the sports centre}, \emph{swimming}, \emph{to twist your ankle}, \emph{to rest}, \emph{to laugh}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: pieces that are real, and pieces that are not}]
Three of this chapter's words look built. Two of them are.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the front piece} \\
\midrule
\textbf{polideportivo} & real — Greek \emph{polýs}, many \\
\textbf{descansar} & real — \emph{des-}, the undoing \\
\textbf{reír} & \textbf{not a piece at all} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The test is not how the word looks; it is whether the rest of the word survives without the piece. Take \emph{poli-} off and \emph{deportivo} stands. Take \emph{des-} off and \emph{cansar} stands. Take \emph{re-} off \emph{reír} and nothing is left, which is the proof that it was never a prefix.

Carry that test forward. It is the one move that keeps morphology from turning into guesswork, and it costs you a second per word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I do swimming at the sports centre on Tuesdays
  \item I twisted my ankle getting out of the pool
  \item \emph{torcemos} and \emph{se tuerce}, and which one breaks the vowel
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You can now say where you exercise, what goes wrong there, what you have to do about it, and how you feel about the whole business.} That is a complete small episode, and it is the shape a clinic conversation and a message to a friend both take.

You also have a second doublet. \textbf{nadar} and \textbf{la natación} are one Latin verb arriving twice, once worn down by mouths and once lifted off the page — and the learned twin is the one on the timetable.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To laugh? (\textbf{Reír}.) To rest? (\textbf{Descansar}.) The sports centre? (\textbf{El polideportivo}.) Which of those three has no prefix? (\textbf{Reír}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(una lesión en el polideportivo) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C438-sintesis-cuerpo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el polideportivo} and \emph{la natación}. Both are on the notice you are about to read, and one of them is cancelled.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read the notice once straight through, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{AVISO — POLIDEPORTIVO MUNICIPAL} Los cursos de \textbf{natación} de la tarde quedan suspendidos del 3 al 10 de octubre por obras en los vestuarios. Las clases de la mañana siguen igual. Para cualquier duda, escriba a avisos@polideportivo.invalid.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item which classes are suspended, and for how long
  \item which classes are not affected
  \item where to write if you have a question
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
Now a message from a friend who went anyway, on a morning.

\begin{quote}
Fui por la mañana y \textbf{me torcí} el tobillo saliendo de la piscina. Nada grave: el médico dice que tengo que \textbf{descansar} tres días. Luego \textbf{nos reímos}, porque llevaba veinte años sin caerme en ningún sitio.
\end{quote}

Notice what each verb is doing. \textbf{Me torcí} puts the injury on the speaker without blaming anyone. \textbf{Descansar} is an instruction with a duration attached. \textbf{Nos reímos} closes the episode, and that closing move is what a Spanish speaker expects at the end of a small misfortune: name it, size it, laugh it off.

A report that stops after \emph{me torcí el tobillo} sounds like a complaint. The same report with \emph{nos reímos} on the end sounds like a story. Same facts, and the last clause decides which one the listener hears.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four sentences: where you went, what you were doing there, what you twisted, and what you have to do now. End it the way the message above ends it.

Then check yourself: did you say \emph{me torcí \textbf{el} tobillo} and not \emph{mi tobillo}?
\end{tcolorbox}
